transcript.content: Hello, it’s nice to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well… I came because things at school have been feeling a bit pointed at me, I suppose. Like staff emails, or the morning announcements—they seem ordinary, but I keep feeling there’s a coded meaning in them about me. My colleagues say, very kindly, “No, everyone got that email,” and they’ll show me, but I still can’t quite shake it.

I know it probably sounds odd. I’ve taught for years, so I’m used to announcements and memos and all that—half of them are about parking or exam schedules, honestly—but lately I hear them and think, “That’s about me, isn’t it?” And then I go over it in my head too much.
Have there been times recently when you felt unusually high, euphoric, or overly full of energy?

I don’t think so… not high, exactly. I mean, sometimes at the start of a school term I get that sort of busy energy, because there are timetables and seating plans and someone’s always lost the keys to the stationery cupboard, but that’s just normal, isn’t it? 

I wouldn’t say euphoric. Mostly I’ve just been trying to get through the days.
Have you been hearing voices when no one else is there?

Yes… sometimes. Not all the time. It’s usually when the house is very quiet, or after the classroom has emptied and I’m tidying up—stacking chairs or wiping the board, that sort of thing. I’ll hear a woman’s voice say my name, quite clearly, or make a little comment about what I’m doing.

The strange thing is I sometimes answer before I’ve even thought about it, like you do when someone calls from the next room. Then I look around and remember there isn’t anyone there. It’s… unsettling.
Have you been feeling depressed most of the day nearly every day recently?

Depressed… I’m not sure I’d put that word on it. I’ve had some low days, I suppose, but then everyone has, especially around exam season—there’s a particular kind of gloom that comes with marking papers in a cold staffroom with bad coffee.

But most of the day, nearly every day… I don’t know. I haven’t really been keeping track of it like that. It’s more that I feel worn down sometimes, if that makes sense, rather than properly depressed.
Have you ever had a period when you needed much less sleep than usual and still felt full of energy?

I don’t think so, no… I’ve always needed my sleep, really. If I don’t get enough, I’m just useless the next day—standing in front of Year 9 trying to remember where I put the worksheets, and they can smell weakness at that age.

There have been nights I’ve slept badly, of course. Marking, worrying, the neighbour’s dog going on and on. But I wouldn’t say I then felt full of energy. More the opposite, really.
Have these experiences been going on for more than a month?

Yes… yes, more than a month. I suppose it’s been about four months now, the coded-message worries and that voice I sometimes answer.

It’s odd, because at first I thought it was just the end of term getting to me—teachers always say September feels like being hit by a cupboard full of paper—but it didn’t really stop after a week or two. It’s been lingering on, really. Four months, give or take.
Have you had any beliefs that others would find very unusual or hard to believe, apart from the coded messages?

Apart from the emails and the announcements… I don’t think there’s anything else, not really.

I mean, that’s the thing I can’t quite shake—the sense that some of the staff emails, or things said in the morning briefing, are sort of… aimed at me, tucked inside normal wording. And I know it sounds odd, because people have shown me, kindly enough, that the email went to everyone. One of the deputy heads even printed the distribution list, which felt a bit humiliating, actually.

But no, I wouldn’t say there are other unusual beliefs beyond that. It’s mainly that school-message business.
Have other people said that your speech or behavior has become noticeably disorganized or hard to follow?

Yes… a bit, I think. Not my speech exactly all the time, but people have noticed I get sort of… stuck.

In lessons, or in the art-fair meetings, I’ll suddenly stop what I’m doing and start rearranging the markers or papers into a particular pattern. It feels important in the moment, like it has to be just so, and then I realise everyone’s waiting and I’ve lost the thread.

And sometimes someone will say something to me and instead of answering properly I’ll just repeat a phrase they’ve used. Like an echo, almost. Then I feel terribly embarrassed, because it interrupts what I’m supposed to be doing. Especially at school—children notice everything, don’t they? Even if they pretend they’re not listening.
During these past four months, have there been any stretches when you felt depressed nearly all day, almost every day, for at least two weeks?

I’m not sure I’d call it that, exactly. I’ve had low days, certainly—everyone does, don’t they? Especially with school being what it is, and the winter term has this way of making the corridors feel grey even when the lights are on.

But nearly all day, almost every day, for two weeks… I don’t know. I haven’t really kept track in that sort of neat way. I suppose I’ve been upset and worn down at times, but I couldn’t honestly say it’s been that clear-cut.
Have these experiences been going on for six months or longer?

Yes… yes, longer than six months, I think. It’s hard to put a pin in it exactly, because it sort of crept in rather than arrived.

But the overall change—how I think, how I manage at work, how I’ve been with people—really started after my youngest left for college. That was about a year and two months ago now. Funny, I still catch myself setting aside the good mugs when they come home, as if that has anything to do with it… but yes, since then, roughly. More than six months.
Have you had a period when you felt unusually euphoric or irritable most of the day, nearly every day, for at least a week?

I don’t think so… not in that sort of clear, week-long way. I can be irritable, certainly—ask anyone who’s been in a staff meeting where the agenda has twelve items and no one’s read the papers—but that feels more like ordinary frustration.

Euphoric… no, I wouldn’t say that. I mean, I’ve had moments where I get quite caught up in something, like planning a lesson or sorting things for the art fair, and then suddenly it’s hours later and I’ve forgotten tea’s gone cold. But feeling unusually high or irritable most of the day, nearly every day for a week… I can’t really say I’ve noticed that.
Before these experiences began, were you diagnosed with any medical or neurological illness?

I don’t think so… not that I can remember being told, anyway. I’ve always been fairly ordinary with that sort of thing—dentist appointments, eye tests, the usual reminders stuck to the fridge and then ignored until the week before.

Medical or neurological illness… I mean, no one sat me down before all this and said there was something like that going on. Unless you count the usual aches from standing in classrooms for years, but that’s not really what you mean, is it?
Have there been times when the voice or the coded-message feeling was happening even though you were not depressed or unusually high at that time?

I’m not sure I’ve separated it out that neatly, if I’m honest. I don’t keep track like that—mood in one column, voices or messages in another. I probably should, my daughter would make a spreadsheet for it, she’s very good with that sort of thing.

But… I don’t know. I can’t say for certain whether it was happening when I was depressed or high, because I’m not always sure what counts as depressed, and I wouldn’t say I get unusually high. The coded-message feeling just sort of comes along sometimes, and I haven’t noticed a clear pattern with mood.
During the past year, was there ever a two-week period when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

I’m not sure, honestly. Two weeks sounds… quite precise, doesn’t it? I know I’ve had low days, especially when school gets on top of me or when the house feels too quiet, but whether it was most of the day nearly every day for a full fortnight… I haven’t really marked it out like that.

I tend to just keep going, you know—make the lunch, answer emails, put the washing on, then suddenly it’s Thursday and I can’t remember what I did on Monday. So I couldn’t confidently say yes to that.
Before these experiences started, did you have a significant head injury?

I don’t think so… not a significant one, anyway. I mean, I’ve bumped my head like anyone does—cupboard doors are vicious things, especially the one above our kettle—but nothing where I was taken off somewhere or told I’d injured my head properly.

Unless you mean something from years and years ago? I wouldn’t have kept track of that very well. But before all this started, no, I can’t remember any serious head injury.
Have there been at least two weeks when you were hearing the voice or feeling messages were aimed at you, even though your mood felt normal for you?

Yes… I think so. I mean, the voice and that feeling that messages are sort of aimed at me has been going on for about four months now, on and off.

Whether my mood was “normal” the whole time—well, normal for me can include being tired and cross because Year 10 haven’t done their homework, you know—but it hasn’t all been during some big low patch or anything like that. So yes, there would have been at least two weeks in there where my mood felt more or less like me and it was still happening.
Since this started, have you found yourself caring much less about things or having much less emotion than usual?

Yes… I suppose I have, though I don’t like saying it because it sounds as if I don’t care, and I do. I still care about my students, and my friends. If one of the girls is upset or a colleague needs help, I’m not made of stone.

But it’s like the warmth has gone a bit flat, or the drive has leaked out somehow. For months, I’ve let things slip—book club, for instance. I used to enjoy arguing about endings and whether the author had cheated, all that nonsense. And I’d been helping plan a theatre trip, but now I just… don’t follow it up unless someone prods me. Even phoning people back feels oddly heavy, which is ridiculous because it’s just a phone call. I can still do things if I’m pushed, but left to myself I tend to let them slide.
During the past year, was there ever a time when you lost interest or pleasure in nearly everything you usually enjoy for at least two weeks?

Yes… though I’m not sure it’s “pleasure in nearly everything,” exactly. I still care about people—my students, my friends. I don’t want them to think I’ve gone cold.

But for many months it’s felt like the warmth and the get-up-and-go have sort of drained out of me. I used to like book club, all the fuss over biscuits and someone always choosing a depressing novel in February—honestly, who does that? And the theatre trip planning, I was meant to help with that too. Now I just let it slide unless someone pushes me.

Even phone calls feel like… too much, somehow. So yes, I suppose there has been a long stretch where I’ve not really enjoyed or pursued the things I normally would.
During that long stretch when your interest and enjoyment dropped, did you also feel sad or low most of the day nearly every day?

I don’t know that I’d call it sad, exactly. Low… maybe sometimes. But “most of the day nearly every day” sounds very precise, and I’m not sure.

It’s more like I’ve been flat and not very sparked by things. I can still go into school and have a perfectly normal conversation about, oh, whether someone’s copied half their coursework from the internet—which they always think you won’t notice, as if we were born yesterday. But underneath it, I suppose I feel dulled rather than weepy.

So… I’m not sure. I wouldn’t want to say yes to being sad nearly every day if that’s not quite it.
Have you had any seizures?

Seizures? I don’t think so. I mean, not that I’m aware of.

When you say seizures, I think of someone collapsing on the floor like in those awful first-aid videos they make us watch at school—half the staff go pale before they’ve even got to the recovery position. I’ve not had anything like that, no. Unless you mean something much smaller or stranger… I’m not sure I’d know what to look for, really.

inference.note: Longitudinal course >6 months with auditory hallucinations, delusions of reference, disorganized behavior, and echolalia supports schizophrenia-spectrum illness. Repeated denial of clear manic episodes and lack of sustained major depressive episodes make schizoaffective disorders less likely but not fully excluded yet. Delusional disorder is less favored because hallucinations/disorganization are present. Organic psychosis remains possible pending medical/substance history.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there have been psychotic symptoms in the context of a medical or neurological condition, to distinguish primary psychotic disorders from organic psychosis.
doctor.question: Before these experiences began, were you diagnosed with any medical or neurological illness?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about prior medical or neurological diagnoses, but the provided symptom profile does not include medical or neurological illness history.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so… not that I can remember being told, anyway. I’ve always been fairly ordinary with that sort of thing—dentist appointments, eye tests, the usual reminders stuck to the fridge and then ignored until the week before.

Medical or neurological illness… I mean, no one sat me down before all this and said there was something like that going on. Unless you count the usual aches from standing in classrooms for years, but that’s not really what you mean, is it?

doctor.intent: Determine whether hallucinations or delusions have occurred in the absence of prominent mood symptoms, to distinguish schizophrenia from schizoaffective disorder.
doctor.question: Have there been times when the voice or the coded-message feeling was happening even though you were not depressed or unusually high at that time?

target_item.reason: The question is about whether psychotic experiences occurred outside depressive or unusually high mood episodes, but the symptom profile does not include mood-episode timing or mood-related context.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’ve separated it out that neatly, if I’m honest. I don’t keep track like that—mood in one column, voices or messages in another. I probably should, my daughter would make a spreadsheet for it, she’s very good with that sort of thing.

But… I don’t know. I can’t say for certain whether it was happening when I was depressed or high, because I’m not always sure what counts as depressed, and I wouldn’t say I get unusually high. The coded-message feeling just sort of comes along sometimes, and I haven’t noticed a clear pattern with mood.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a sustained major depressive episode, which would help distinguish schizophrenia from schizoaffective disorder, depressive type.
doctor.question: During the past year, was there ever a two-week period when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

target_item.reason: The question is specifically about a two-week period of depressed mood, which is not covered by the provided symptom profiles; negative symptoms involve reduced motivation/emotional expression but are not the same as depressed mood.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure, honestly. Two weeks sounds… quite precise, doesn’t it? I know I’ve had low days, especially when school gets on top of me or when the house feels too quiet, but whether it was most of the day nearly every day for a full fortnight… I haven’t really marked it out like that.

I tend to just keep going, you know—make the lunch, answer emails, put the washing on, then suddenly it’s Thursday and I can’t remember what I did on Monday. So I couldn’t confidently say yes to that.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a history of a brain injury that could point to an organic psychotic disorder rather than a primary psychotic disorder.
doctor.question: Before these experiences started, did you have a significant head injury?

target_item.reason: The question asks about a prior significant head injury, which is medical/neurological history and is not covered by any listed symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so… not a significant one, anyway. I mean, I’ve bumped my head like anyone does—cupboard doors are vicious things, especially the one above our kettle—but nothing where I was taken off somewhere or told I’d injured my head properly.

Unless you mean something from years and years ago? I wouldn’t have kept track of that very well. But before all this started, no, I can’t remember any serious head injury.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there have been prominent psychotic symptoms occurring in the absence of mood episodes, to distinguish schizophrenia from schizoaffective disorder.
doctor.question: Have there been at least two weeks when you were hearing the voice or feeling messages were aimed at you, even though your mood felt normal for you?

target_item.name: Psychotic Symptoms Duration
target_item.manifestation: The coded-message worries and the voice I sometimes answer have been happening for about four months.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about whether the voice and coded-message experiences lasted for at least two weeks, which is most directly about the duration of the psychotic symptoms.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think so. I mean, the voice and that feeling that messages are sort of aimed at me has been going on for about four months now, on and off.

Whether my mood was “normal” the whole time—well, normal for me can include being tired and cross because Year 10 haven’t done their homework, you know—but it hasn’t all been during some big low patch or anything like that. So yes, there would have been at least two weeks in there where my mood felt more or less like me and it was still happening.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has had prominent negative symptoms, which would support schizophrenia over delusional disorder or schizoaffective disorder.
doctor.question: Since this started, have you found yourself caring much less about things or having much less emotion than usual?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: I still care about my students and friends, but for many months it has felt like the warmth and drive have drained out of me, so I let book club, theater planning, and even simple phone calls slide unless someone pushes me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about reduced caring and reduced emotional expression since the onset, which directly matches negative symptoms.

patient.answer:
Yes… I suppose I have, though I don’t like saying it because it sounds as if I don’t care, and I do. I still care about my students, and my friends. If one of the girls is upset or a colleague needs help, I’m not made of stone.

But it’s like the warmth has gone a bit flat, or the drive has leaked out somehow. For months, I’ve let things slip—book club, for instance. I used to enjoy arguing about endings and whether the author had cheated, all that nonsense. And I’d been helping plan a theatre trip, but now I just… don’t follow it up unless someone prods me. Even phoning people back feels oddly heavy, which is ridiculous because it’s just a phone call. I can still do things if I’m pushed, but left to myself I tend to let them slide.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether there has been a major depressive episode, which is the key remaining discriminator between schizophrenia and depressive-type schizoaffective disorder given psychosis outside mood episodes and no evidence of mania.
doctor.question: During the past year, was there ever a time when you lost interest or pleasure in nearly everything you usually enjoy for at least two weeks?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: I still care about my students and friends, but for many months it has felt like the warmth and drive have drained out of me, so I let book club, theater planning, and even simple phone calls slide unless someone pushes me.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about loss of interest or pleasure in usual activities, which most directly matches diminished motivation/social interest in the negative symptoms profile.

patient.answer:
Yes… though I’m not sure it’s “pleasure in nearly everything,” exactly. I still care about people—my students, my friends. I don’t want them to think I’ve gone cold.

But for many months it’s felt like the warmth and the get-up-and-go have sort of drained out of me. I used to like book club, all the fuss over biscuits and someone always choosing a depressing novel in February—honestly, who does that? And the theatre trip planning, I was meant to help with that too. Now I just let it slide unless someone pushes me.

Even phone calls feel like… too much, somehow. So yes, I suppose there has been a long stretch where I’ve not really enjoyed or pursued the things I normally would.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a sustained major depressive episode, which would help distinguish schizophrenia from schizoaffective disorder, depressive type.
doctor.question: During that long stretch when your interest and enjoyment dropped, did you also feel sad or low most of the day nearly every day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about feeling sad or low most of the day nearly every day, which is a depressive mood symptom. The provided profile includes reduced interest/drive under Negative_Symptoms, but it does not include persistent depressed mood.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I’d call it sad, exactly. Low… maybe sometimes. But “most of the day nearly every day” sounds very precise, and I’m not sure.

It’s more like I’ve been flat and not very sparked by things. I can still go into school and have a perfectly normal conversation about, oh, whether someone’s copied half their coursework from the internet—which they always think you won’t notice, as if we were born yesterday. But underneath it, I suppose I feel dulled rather than weepy.

So… I’m not sure. I wouldn’t want to say yes to being sad nearly every day if that’s not quite it.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms may be due to an underlying medical cause, helping distinguish a primary psychotic disorder from F06.2.
doctor.question: Have you had any seizures?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about seizures, which are not covered by any item in the provided symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Seizures? I don’t think so. I mean, not that I’m aware of.

When you say seizures, I think of someone collapsing on the floor like in those awful first-aid videos they make us watch at school—half the staff go pale before they’ve even got to the recovery position. I’ve not had anything like that, no. Unless you mean something much smaller or stranger… I’m not sure I’d know what to look for, really.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has a chronic psychotic illness with characteristic schizophrenic symptoms: auditory hallucinations, referential/persecutory delusional ideas about coded messages, disorganized behavior/speech phenomena, and negative symptoms with functional decline. Duration exceeds 6 months, and there is no clear evidence of sustained manic or major depressive episodes sufficient for schizoaffective disorder. A primary medical/neurological cause is not supported by the interview. Delusional disorder is less likely because hallucinations, disorganization, and negative symptoms are present.
